title: First Brands: $5 Billion in Sales, $12 Million in Cash
summary:
First Brands collapse explained from court and bankruptcy records.

The owner of Fram, Autolite and Raybestos sold about $5 billion of car parts a year. In September 2025 it filed for bankruptcy with $12 million in cash and more than $9 billion in liabilities. Using the US Attorney's charges, bankruptcy filings and lenders' own statements, we explain how invoice finance works, what prosecutors allege happened, what is still disputed, and who paid. Patrick and Edward James deny the charges and are presumed innocent; their trial is scheduled for February 2027.

scenes.say: A car-parts company selling five billion dollars a year went bankrupt with twelve million dollars in the bank.
And more than nine billion dollars of debts.
You've probably used its products. Fram oil filters. Autolite spark plugs. Raybestos brakes.
Prosecutors say the money was raised with fake invoices and debts hidden from lenders. The founder and his brother deny it. Their trial is set for February 2027.
So where did the money go? And how did some of the biggest names in finance miss it? Keep that second question in mind.

visual.text: Where did First Brands’ money go?

scenes.say: We use the court record: the US Attorney's charges, bankruptcy court filings, lenders' own statements, and reporting on the case. Where something is only alleged, we'll say so.

visual.title: The paperwork
items: US Attorney (New York) indictment announcement, Jan 2026
Trade and business press on the case

scenes.say: Chapter 1. Built on borrowed money.
Patrick James founded the business in Ohio in 2013. It was then called Crowne Group.

visual.text: Crowne Group founded in Ohio by Patrick James
visual.src: Wikipedia: First Brands Group (pointer only, verify)

scenes.src: Wikipedia: First Brands Group (pointer only, verify)

scenes.say: It bought windscreen-wiper maker Trico, then about two dozen more parts makers, mostly with borrowed money. In 2020 it renamed itself First Brands Group.

visual.text: Renamed First Brands Group after ~24 debt-funded acquisitions
visual.src: Wikipedia: First Brands Group (pointer only, verify)

scenes.src: Wikipedia: First Brands Group (pointer only, verify)

scenes.say: From the outside, it looked boring in a good way. Cars always need filters, wipers and brake pads.
But a business like that has a cash problem built in. And the way it solved that problem is the heart of this story.
Chapter 2. Selling tomorrow's money today.
When a parts maker ships to a retailer, the retailer often pays months later. That unpaid bill is called a receivable.
Instead of waiting, the company can sell the bill to a finance firm, called a factor, for a bit less than it's worth. The factor collects the full amount later.

visual.title: How factoring works
items: 2. Factor pays most of it now

scenes.say: This is legal and very common. A related version, used to pay suppliers early, is called supply-chain finance.

visual.text: Factoring and supply-chain finance are normal, legal tools

scenes.say: It only works if two things are true. The invoice is real. And it's sold only once.
Hold on to those two rules. Prosecutors say First Brands broke both of them.
Chapter 3. The deal that asked one question too many.
By August 2025, First Brands had about five point six billion dollars of corporate debt on its balance sheet, and a refinancing deal in the works.
Investors asked for a deeper check, including a quality-of-earnings report. According to the investment firm OHA, that review exposed expensive, risky financing that hadn't been clear before.

visual.text: increasingly risky and expensive working capital financing
visual.by: OHA, on what the diligence found

scenes.say: The deal collapsed. Within three weeks, the price of the company's main loan fell by nearly eighty-three per cent.

visual.label: fall in first-lien term loan price, within three weeks

scenes.say: OHA said some of the off-balance-sheet financing carried interest rates above thirty per cent.
On the twenty-eighth of September 2025, First Brands filed for bankruptcy in Texas.

visual.text: Chapter 11 filing, Southern District of Texas

scenes.say: It reported about five billion dollars in annual sales, twelve million dollars in cash, and more than nine billion dollars in liabilities.
Chapter 4. Up to two point three billion dollars.
Ten days after the filing, Raistone, a finance platform that had arranged funding for First Brands, asked the court to appoint an independent examiner.

visual.text: Raistone asks for an independent examiner

scenes.say: Its filing said up to two point three billion dollars in assets were unaccounted for.

visual.text: up to $2.3 billion in assets unaccounted for

scenes.say: It said that after the bankruptcy began, the company had collected about one point nine billion dollars on invoices that others had already bought, but hadn't passed it on.
Asked how much was in the accounts meant to hold that money, a company lawyer answered: zero dollars.

visual.label: in the segregated accounts, per a company lawyer

scenes.say: Big names were exposed. Jefferies said its own share of one affected fund was forty-three million dollars, and that nobody at the bank had known of any fraud.

visual.text: Nobody at Jefferies was aware of fraudulent activity at First Brands

scenes.say: Chapter 5. The indictment.
On the twenty-ninth of January 2026, federal prosecutors in New York charged Patrick James and his brother Edward, a former senior executive. Both were arrested in Ohio that day.

visual.text: Patrick and Edward James charged and arrested

scenes.say: These are accusations. Both men pleaded not guilty and are presumed innocent.

visual.text: merely accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent

scenes.say: Prosecutors allege that from at least 2018, the company used fake and inflated invoices to raise money from factors, including on bills that didn't exist.
One example in court filings: an invoice worth eight thousand nine hundred and seventy-six dollars was allegedly sold to one factor as seventeen thousand eight hundred dollars.
Three days later, prosecutors say, the same invoice was sold to another factor as four hundred and sixty-three thousand dollars.
They also allege the same collateral was pledged two or three times, so several lenders thought they had a claim on the same thing.

visual.label: times collateral was pledged, as alleged

scenes.say: Then there were the round trips. Money that financers thought would pay suppliers was allegedly routed back to First Brands, to cover interest, rent and running costs.
Internally, the release says, these were called corporate initiatives.

visual.by: internal name, per the US Attorney

scenes.say: Prosecutors also allege that companies controlled by Patrick James took on inventory loans that were hidden from the senior lenders.
In July 2025, according to the indictment as reported, a senior executive told a lender there was no off-balance-sheet financing. Prosecutors put it at about two billion dollars.
Prosecutors say Patrick James received at least hundreds of millions of dollars in his personal accounts. His lawyers dispute the spending claims made against him.

visual.title: Where the money went
lines: Alleged: hundreds of millions to personal accounts
Company civil suit lists rent, a chef, a trainer

scenes.say: Chapter 6. Brother against brother.
Two insiders have already pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate: executive Peter Andrew Brumbergs in January 2026, and former chief financial officer Stephen Graham in March.
Graham had been finance chief since 2014. He's expected to testify.
In September 2026, both brothers asked for separate trials. Patrick's lawyers say Edward ran the alleged fraud. Edward's lawyers say Patrick controlled the company and Edward didn't know.
A jury will decide, not this video. The trial is scheduled for February 2027.

visual.text: Trial scheduled, Judge Analisa Torres, Manhattan

scenes.say: Chapter 7. Who paid.
In January 2026, the company began winding down Autolite, Brake Parts Inc and Cardone. Bloomberg reported at least four thousand jobs already lost in North America.

visual.label: North American jobs lost, Bloomberg, Jan 2026

scenes.say: Other businesses were sold off. In August 2026, the bankruptcy judge rejected the rescue plan and converted the case into a Chapter 7 liquidation. In plain English: it's being sold in pieces.
That rejected plan relied on about two billion dollars of future lawsuit recoveries from former insiders, mostly by the end of 2028.

visual.label: projected clawbacks in the rejected plan, by end-2028

scenes.say: Our analysis.
Lesson one. Compare cash with sales. Five billion dollars of sales and twelve million in the bank means a company living invoice to invoice.
Lesson two. Debt you can't see is still debt. Off-balance-sheet financing doesn't appear in the headline numbers. That's exactly why lenders should ask about it.

visual.text: Debt you can't see is still debt

scenes.say: Lesson three. When every lender sees only its own slice, nobody sees the whole picture. No single factor could check whether an invoice had already been sold to someone else.
Hidden debt is a pattern on this channel. Patisserie Valerie's chairman said he hadn't known about two bank overdrafts. That case file is on screen now.
The First Brands trial is set for February. Subscribe if you want the follow-up when a jury decides.
